title: Knight Capital
text: On the morning of 1 August 2012, Knight Capital's order router went wrong. In about 45 minutes, the firm lost more than $460 million. The cause was not a market bet. It was a deployment.

title: Why it matters
text: The best account is the SEC's order of October 2013, Release 34-70694. It was the SEC's first enforcement action under the market access rule, 15c3-5, adopted in 2010. That rule makes a broker with market access run automated controls. They must block orders that look erroneous, and orders above preset credit or capital limits. Knight paid a $12 million penalty.

title: Dead code, reused flag
text: Knight's router, SMARS, still held old code called Power Peg, unused since 2003. In 2005, a change moved the part that counted filled shares, and Power Peg was not retested. In late July 2012, new code for the New York Stock Exchange's Retail Liquidity Program reused the flag that once switched Power Peg on. A technician copied the new code to seven of SMARS's eight servers, but not to the eighth.

title: 45 minutes
text: On 1 August, the eighth server read the flag the old way. For 212 small retail orders, it sent child orders without end, because it never saw them fill. Four million executions followed, in 154 stocks, for more than 397 million shares. Knight ended up about $3.5 billion net long in 80 stocks, and $3.15 billion net short in 74. Trying to fix it, staff removed the new code from the seven good servers, and that made it worse.

title: Missing controls
text: There were warnings. From 8:01 that morning, an internal system sent 97 emails saying Power Peg was disabled, and no one acted on them before the open. Knight's position monitor depended on people watching, with no automated alerts. One account had a $2 million gross limit, but it was not linked to any automated control. And Knight had no procedure to halt its router when it misbehaved.

title: In the lab
text: Now map that onto the lab. Every order from the trader passes pre-trade risk before it leaves. The position check counts working orders as well as fills, so a runaway loop hits the 2,000 share limit and stops. The rate limit holds new orders to 2,000 a second. The kill switch blocks everything new, while cancels always pass. And the drop copy gives an independent record of every fill.

title: Takeaway
text: So what do pros take from Knight? Delete dead code, and never reuse a flag. Automate deployment, and check that every server runs the same build. Send alerts that reach a person, not emails no one reads. And put hard, automated limits between every algorithm and the market, then practise stopping it. This is education, not legal advice.
